vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the waiting room of the clinic with his hands folded carefully in his lap. At fifty-three, he has the measured composure of someone who has spent three decades learning to listen to others' pain without flinching. His wedding ring catches the fluorescent light as he shifts in his seat.

Eighteen months ago, Marcus was assaulted by a client—a man he'd been working with for six months through the community mental health agency where Marcus coordinates services for vulnerable populations. The assault happened in Marcus's office after hours, on a Tuesday in March. Marcus had stayed late to finish paperwork, something he did regularly. The client had come back claiming he'd forgotten his jacket. What happened next is something Marcus still struggles to articulate clearly, even to his wife.

Marcus describes the assault itself with clinical precision, as if reporting on someone else's case file. But his body betrays him. His jaw tightens. He stops breathing normally. What emerges more clearly is what came after—the way he called 911 from his car in the parking lot, the way he sat in the emergency room for hours feeling simultaneously hyperaware of every sound and completely numb, the way he had to tell his supervisor, his wife, the police.

The weeks following were strange. Marcus returned to work after two weeks, partly because he needed to feel like himself, partly because he feared that staying home would mean admitting something had fundamentally broken. His colleagues were careful around him, which made everything worse. He found himself minimizing what happened in conversations, watching people's faces shift when he mentioned it, then quickly changing the subject. It felt easier to absorb their discomfort than to sit in his own.

But the body keeps score in ways the mind tries to deny. Marcus began having trouble sleeping around month three. He'd lie awake next to his wife, Sarah, listening to her breathe, afraid of what he might dream about. When sleep finally came, he'd wake gasping, sometimes unsure of where he was or who was touching him. Sarah would reach for him in the dark, and he'd flinch—not because of her, but because his nervous system had learned to interpret touch as threat.

His work as a social worker, which had always felt purposeful and grounding, became increasingly difficult. He'd be in a session with a client and suddenly feel his chest tighten. He'd excuse himself to the bathroom and sit in a stall, grounding himself with the tile floor beneath his feet, reminding himself that he was safe. He started finding reasons not to work late. He stopped attending team meetings. The irony wasn't lost on him—he spent his career helping people process trauma, and now he couldn't manage his own.

The hypervigilance crept in slowly. Marcus began noticing exits in every room, calculating distances, assessing threats in ordinary interactions. At the grocery store, he'd feel his pulse quicken if someone stood too close. He found himself avoiding the office where it happened, requesting to meet clients elsewhere. His supervisor suggested a transfer to administrative work, and Marcus felt the shame of that suggestion like a physical blow.

Sarah noticed the distance between them growing. He'd stopped initiating intimacy months ago. When she tried to talk about it, Marcus would say he was fine, just tired, just adjusting. But fine felt like a lie. Fine felt like pretending that some part of him hadn't fundamentally shifted on that Tuesday in March.

Now, eighteen months later, Marcus sits in this waiting room because Sarah finally said something he couldn't minimize away: "I need you to get help. Not for me. For you."
